strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging video-editing problem: controllable object insertion with camera motion, occlusions, and scene-dependent illumination. The supplied examples are visually compelling, particularly around occluders and moving support surfaces.

Although no contribution type is declared, this work is best assessed as Applied/Systems rather than as a fundamentally new algorithm. From that perspective, combining monocular 4D reconstruction, interactive 3D placement, scene-flow propagation, first-frame inpainting, and video diffusion is a coherent and practically motivated design.

ROSE++ offers a sensible way to repurpose paired object-removal data for insertion, including supervision for shadows and other effects outside the object mask. The VLM-generated reference-image idea also addresses the train-test mismatch caused by using crops from target videos.

The paper includes component ablations, a scene-flow example, a user study, implementation details, and quantitative measurements of identity, background preservation, temporal quality, and occlusion-related consistency. The full system consistently improves most reported metrics over the two evaluated commercial tools.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not controlled. InsertAnywhere receives precise interactive 3D position, orientation, scale, a geometry-derived mask sequence, and an edited first frame, while Pika-Pro and Kling appear to receive only an object image and a coarse text instruction. Their failures to select the intended location therefore do not establish that the proposed generation model or 4D representation is superior under comparable control. This substantially weakens the main claim of significant outperformance.

The evaluation omits the most relevant academic methods discussed in the paper, including Anything in Any Scene, INVI, VideoAnyDoor, DreamInsert, GenProp, and mask-conditioned video inpainting alternatives. At minimum, same-mask comparisons against VACE and other inpainting/propagation baselines are needed to isolate the value of ROSE++ fine-tuning and first-frame guidance.

Several crucial technical steps are underspecified or internally ambiguous. The paper begins with 2D optical flow, says it is lifted to 3D without defining that operation, and then adds V directly to a 3D point in Eq. 2. Averaging nearby flow supports translation only and does not justify the claimed handling of rotation or more complex support motion. Likewise, the visibility test needed to obtain occlusion-aware silhouettes against reconstructed scene geometry, rasterization details, SAM2 prompting, and failure handling are not described.

The evidence for 4D mask generation is limited. There is no direct mask/trajectory accuracy benchmark, comparison against 2D tracking or alternative reconstruction methods, systematic evaluation by occlusion severity or camera motion, or analysis of sensitivity to depth, pose, flow, SAM2, and single-view reconstruction errors. One qualitative scene-flow example and small downstream metric changes do not validate the broad robustness claims.

VOIBench and the reported metrics are insufficiently documented. The video sources, licenses, selection procedure, duration, resolution, object-pair construction, splits, prompt protocol, mask production for subject-only scoring, and benchmark release status are absent. “Multi-View Consistency” is not formally defined, despite being central to the geometric claim. No uncertainty, repeated-run variance, or significance test is reported.

ROSE++ is not reproducible from the manuscript: its size and split are missing, as are the exact image-generation model/version, values of n, m, and N, generation settings, filtering process, and DINO implementation. Equation 4 refers to full sampled frames even though the prose describes masked object crops. Potential leakage or overlap between ROSE++, pretrained models, and VOIBench is not examined.

The ablations confound multiple changes and do not isolate key choices. There is no comparison of LoRA training on ROSE versus ROSE++, removal of first-frame guidance under the final training setup, alternative reference construction beyond one random-crop variant, or matched-mask baseline. Improvements attributed specifically to illumination supervision are demonstrated mainly through selected images rather than a targeted quantitative measure.

The user study samples only 10% of the test videos, but the exact number of evaluated outputs and vote aggregation are unclear; the reported 1.82% increments are difficult to reconcile with the stated 20-participant protocol. Participant expertise, blinding beyond display-order randomization, and uncertainty are also omitted.

The system is computationally elaborate and depends on several large pretrained components, yet inference time, memory requirements, per-stage latency, reconstruction failures, and manual interaction cost are not reported. These omissions matter for the claimed production applicability.

Overall, this is a promising systems prototype, but the unequal baselines, absent academic comparisons, underdefined benchmark, and incomplete specification of the core geometry pipeline prevent a convincing scientific case in its current form. A controlled evaluation with identical spatial conditioning and substantially stronger reproducibility details could change the assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer-vision problem: controllable video object insertion with temporal geometry, occlusion, and illumination consistency.

The two-stage design is intuitive: 4D reconstruction supplies user-controllable masks, while first-frame-guided video diffusion handles appearance synthesis. The interactive placement interface could be useful in production workflows.

Reversing ROSE object-removal pairs to obtain insertion supervision is a sensible use of existing data, and generating clean reference-object images attempts to reduce the train–test mismatch caused by using video crops.

The paper provides quantitative comparisons, component ablations, qualitative examples involving camera motion and occlusion, and a small user study. The reported improvements over Pika-Pro and Kling are substantial on most metrics.
Implementation details such as the video backbone, resolution, LoRA rank, optimization length, inference steps, hardware, and training time are reported.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the technical novelty is limited. The system largely composes Uni4D, single-view 3D reconstruction, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, an image inpainter, VACE, and LoRA. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its algorithmic contribution from system integration or demonstrate that the proposed coupling provides a broadly reusable technical advance.

The central 4D propagation method is underspecified and internally inconsistent. The text says that 2D flow is lifted into 3D and averaged to update the object centroid, whereas Eq. (2) applies a spatially varying flow to every object point. The lifting procedure, depth correspondence, treatment of camera-induced motion, visibility tests, value of K, and accumulated-drift handling are not defined. Translation alone also cannot model rotations of an object supported by a moving surface.

Claims of reliable occlusion handling are not adequately validated. Reprojection is said to rasterize “visible” points, but depth ordering against dynamic scene geometry is unexplained. No mask, depth-ordering, trajectory, or occlusion-boundary ground truth is used to measure geometric accuracy; the evidence consists mainly of selected output frames and a vaguely defined downstream score.

The comparison is incomplete and potentially unfair. Although the related-work section cites multiple academic insertion and propagation methods—including AnyDoor/Anything in Any Scene, INVI, GenProp, VideoAnyDoor, and DreamInsert—the experiments compare only against two closed-source, prompt-driven commercial systems with different control interfaces. This does not establish superiority over the relevant research state of the art.

Several metrics and protocols are insufficiently specified. “Multi-View Consistency” is attributed to VBench but is not formally defined, so its connection to occlusion correctness is unclear. CLIP/DINO similarity and generic VBench quality metrics do not directly measure geometric placement, shadows, reflections, or illumination adaptation. There are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests for the relatively small 100-output benchmark.

The evidence for ROSE++ and illumination modeling is weak. Dataset size, filtering, object/category distribution, splits, VLM identity and settings, candidate counts, and generation failure rates are omitted. The illumination and shadow claims rely primarily on two qualitative examples; there is no controlled photometric evaluation or equal-data baseline showing that VLM-generated references, rather than additional fine-tuning, are responsible for the gains.

The ablations are sequential and confounded. They do not separately evaluate reconstruction quality, scene-flow propagation against a static or 2D-tracking alternative, SAM2 mask refinement, first-frame inpainter choice, or ROSE++ supervision under matched training budgets. The random-crop comparison reports only one downstream metric.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the first-frame insertion model is not clearly identified, important hyperparameters n, m, and K are absent, prompts and settings for the main commercial comparison are only partially described, and no release commitment or licensing/provenance discussion is given for ROSE++, VOIBench, or the crawled reference objects.

The user study samples only 10% of the test outputs and omits participant recruitment, assignment counts, statistical analysis, and agreement measures. The reported percentage increments are also difficult to reconcile with 20 participants and the stated sampling protocol.

The paper overstates “commercial” or “production” quality without evaluating failure cases, runtime/memory at inference, robustness to reconstruction errors, moving or deforming supports, large viewpoint changes, or out-of-domain objects. It also omits discussion of misuse and disclosure concerns associated with realistic product placement. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing technical detail and inadequate, unfairly scoped validation are consequential enough to favor rejection.

strengths: InsertAnywhere addresses an important and practically relevant video-editing problem: controllable object insertion with perspective changes, occlusion, illumination, and shadows. The combination of 4D-aware placement with diffusion-based synthesis is well motivated.

The user-controlled 3D placement interface and propagation of a single initial placement into a full mask sequence offer useful control over object position, scale, and orientation. The qualitative examples show notably better background preservation and occlusion handling than Pika-Pro and Kling.

Reformulating ROSE object-removal data into insertion supervision is a clever way to obtain examples containing object-induced shadows and lighting changes. The VLM-generated reference-image strategy also addresses the train-test mismatch associated with using crops from target videos.

The experiments include component ablations, a reference-generation ablation, quantitative comparisons, and a perceptual study. The complete system substantially improves CLIP-I, DINO-I, and multi-view consistency over the evaluated commercial systems; the supplementary results are visually compelling.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, and it provides useful training details, including the Wan2.1-VACE-14B backbone, LoRA rank, optimization schedule, resolution, sequence length, hardware, and training time.
weaknesses: The comparison is too narrow to substantiate the strongest claims. Only two closed commercial systems are evaluated, apparently through text prompts rather than the explicit masks and 3D placement available to the proposed method. Academic VOI or propagation methods cited by the paper—including AnyDoor-style video methods, INVI, DreamInsert, VideoAnyDoor, and GenProp—are not compared. This input/control mismatch makes the headline superiority result difficult to interpret fairly.

VOIBench is small—50 source clips with two objects each—and its construction, selection criteria, licenses, train/test independence, and planned release are not specified. The new multi-view consistency metric is not formally defined, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Several VBench gains over Kling are quite small, while Kling has slightly higher motion smoothness.

Important method details are underspecified. In particular, the procedure for lifting 2D optical flow into 3D, selecting and updating neighboring points over time, resolving visibility with scene depth, and rasterizing sparse reconstructed objects into masks is not sufficiently precise. Applying an averaged local translation to the object is also unlikely to model rotations, deformation, support changes, or independently moving neighbors reliably.

ROSE++ lacks basic reproducibility information such as its number of clips and objects, category distribution, splits, the values of n and m, the exact VLM/version and generation settings, quality filtering, and release status. Dependence on a proprietary VLM and a 14B video backbone further limits reproducibility.

The user-study accounting appears internally inconsistent: sampling 10% of 100 generated videos with 20 participants should produce vote percentages in 0.5-point increments, yet Table 4 reports values such as 1.82% and 79.09%. The paper should clarify the actual number of evaluated videos, assignments per participant, aggregation procedure, ties, and statistical uncertainty.

The paper provides almost no systematic failure analysis. Likely limitations—including inaccurate monocular geometry, fast or nonrigid motion, reflective or transparent surfaces, severe/long occlusions, and errors caused by averaging neighboring scene flow—are not evaluated. Consequently, claims of production or commercial-level quality are stronger than the presented evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant computer-vision problem: controllable video object insertion under camera motion, dynamic occlusion, and scene-dependent lighting. Combining 4D placement with optics-aware synthesis is a coherent and potentially impactful direction.

The proposed system is technically well motivated. A single user-defined 3D placement is propagated using reconstructed geometry and local scene flow, while first-frame anchoring and mask conditioning provide useful appearance and spatial control.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is an interesting contribution: training with an extended mask as a stop-gradient feature target offers a plausible way to produce shadows and reflections at inference time while retaining a tight user mask. The held-out ROSE++ evaluation reports a substantial optics-region PSNR improvement from 19.91 to 27.24 dB over the same model without the alignment loss.

The evaluation is unusually broad, including commercial and open-source systems, a strong VACE baseline supplied with the authors' masks and first frame, progressive component ablations, paired synthetic evaluation, qualitative comparisons, and two user studies. The full method performs best on five of six main quantitative metrics and is strongly preferred for object realism and overall naturalness in the primary user study.

The presentation is clear and visually compelling. The supplementary material reports training and inference costs, baseline input adaptations, additional qualitative cases, and useful implementation details.
weaknesses: The central geometric claim is insufficiently evaluated. VOIBench has no ground-truth object trajectories, masks, depth ordering, or poses, and the reported CLIP/DINO and VBench metrics do not measure placement accuracy, support-surface attachment, or occlusion correctness. Scene-flow propagation is validated mainly through one qualitative comparison, with no quantitative comparison to 2D tracking, static-world placement, alternative flow aggregation, or ground-truth masks.

The optics evidence is strongest only on 25 held-out synthetic ROSE++ samples. It is unclear whether train/test splitting prevents scene or object leakage, and the paper provides no paired real-world optics benchmark. Generic VBench metrics on VOIBench cannot establish that shadows or reflections are physically correct; the optics-focused user study helps, but reports no confidence intervals or significance tests and uses clips explicitly selected for strong effects.

Important reproducibility details are missing: ROSE++'s total size and splits, reference-candidate count, mask-difference threshold and morphology settings, K in KNN propagation, visibility/depth-testing procedure, alignment-loss weight and selected layers, LoRA target modules, benchmark-generation protocol, and commercial-system versions/settings. The claim that ROSE++ and VOIBench will be open-sourced is valuable, but the manuscript itself does not provide enough information to reconstruct them.

The main benchmark is introduced and evaluated by the authors, with contextually relevant reference objects described as 'crawled.' There is little discussion of curation, licensing, duplicate removal, or possible overlap with training data. Commercial and mask-free baselines also receive inherently weaker control signals than the proposed method, so their comparison should be interpreted cautiously, although the matched VACE comparisons partially mitigate this concern.

Several conclusions are overstated. An average KNN scene-flow update does not guarantee correct motion when nearby points belong to multiple independently moving surfaces, and the paper does not study failures from monocular depth, camera-pose, flow, TRELLIS geometry, or SAM2 errors. Consequently, claims such as 'production-grade,' 'guarantees precise spatial control,' and automatic handling of complex dynamics are stronger than the presented evidence. The limitations section mentions soft-body physics but omits these more immediate failure modes.

The alignment mechanism is underspecified conceptually: the extended-mask teacher and fine-mask student share backbone parameters, yet the paper does not clearly explain the complete training objective or how teacher representations remain a stable target. Ablations show its benefit, but analysis of loss weight, layer choice, computational overhead, and possible background changes would make the contribution substantially more convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: controllable video object insertion with temporal geometry, occlusion handling, background preservation, and optical interactions considered jointly.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and technically plausible. It combines 4D reconstruction, user-controlled 3D placement, scene-flow propagation, first-frame anchoring, and mask-conditioned diffusion in a useful end-to-end system.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is an interesting idea: training a fine-mask representation against a stop-gradient extended-mask branch provides a simple way to model effects outside the object boundary without requiring that extended mask at inference.

The evaluation is broad in form, covering commercial and open-source baselines, component ablations, paired reconstruction metrics, qualitative examples, and two user studies. The reported gains in subject fidelity, image quality, and human preference are substantial.
The paper is generally clear and includes useful implementation details such as the backbone, LoRA configuration, training cost, resolution, and inference time.
weaknesses: The geometric contribution is inadequately validated. Despite strong claims of geometrically grounded, occlusion-robust placement, the paper reports no mask IoU, trajectory error, depth-ordering accuracy, pose error, or controlled comparison against tracking, propagation, or 4D-reconstruction alternatives. Its principal evidence is a few selected qualitative sequences and an ablation against a static or bounding-box mask.

The propagation model is much weaker than the claims suggest. Averaging the scene flow of the K nearest points estimates translation only; it does not model object rotation, articulated or deforming supports, attachment boundaries, or multiple nearby surfaces. The paper neither analyzes these failure cases nor specifies a robust mechanism for choosing K and preventing flow from unrelated surfaces from contaminating the motion.

Occlusion handling is underspecified. Equation (5) merely projects object points, while the text claims that reprojection “naturally” accounts for occlusion. No explicit depth test or visibility-compositing procedure against scene geometry is described, and the subsequent use of SAM 2 does not by itself establish correct foreground/background ordering.

The central optics result rests on a very small paired test of only 25 synthetic ROSE++ samples. This does not convincingly establish real-world shadow and reflection accuracy or generalization. VOIBench uses generic CLIP, DINO, and VBench measures that are not direct metrics of optical consistency; real-world evidence for the main optics claim is therefore largely subjective.

ROSE++ and VOIBench are insufficiently documented for claimed dataset/benchmark contributions. The manuscript omits the size and composition of ROSE++, train/validation/test splits, candidate-generation count and thresholds, overlap controls, licensing and provenance details, and concrete release information. VOIBench similarly lacks source, annotation, object-selection, difficulty-distribution, and reproducible evaluation-protocol details.

Baseline fairness remains problematic because methods receive substantially different control modalities. Commercial systems receive text prompts, several baselines receive edited first frames, and VACE receives the authors' masks and first frame. These comparisons may reflect interface and conditioning advantages rather than the proposed techniques. The paper also does not compare against several directly relevant mask-conditioned insertion systems discussed in related work.

The alignment method is not specified sufficiently for reproduction: the selected transformer layers, feature normalization and weighting, alignment coefficient, extended-mask threshold and morphology parameters, and complete diffusion-training objective are absent. It is also unclear how the extended-mask teacher branch is optimized and why shared-weight feature matching avoids trivial or undesirable solutions.

The ablation does not cleanly isolate all claimed contributions. Configurations are cumulative, the first-frame anchor is itself produced by a strong external insertion model, and there is no comparison against simpler strategies such as mask dilation, directly training with stochastic expanded masks, predicting an optical-effect mask, or permitting generation in a soft boundary band.

The user studies omit uncertainty estimates, significance tests, participant demographics, clip-to-participant assignment, and detailed trial counts. The optics-focused study uses 50 explicitly selected shadow/reflection-rich clips, which can favor the proposed method and is not a substitute for an independently sampled real-world test.

The paper repeatedly uses unsupported absolute language such as “production-grade,” “guarantees,” and “accurately handles” despite dependence on fallible monocular depth, camera pose, flow, segmentation, image-to-3D generation, and first-frame editing. The limitations section mentions only complex physical interaction and does not discuss these more immediate failure sources, computational requirements, synthetic-to-real bias, or misuse risks.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper presents a compelling and practically relevant framework that jointly addresses two important VOI problems: geometrically grounded placement and optical interactions outside the object mask.

The combination of 4D reconstruction, user-controlled 3D anchoring, scene-flow propagation, first-frame conditioning, and optics-aware generation forms a coherent end-to-end system. The single-placement interface is especially useful for challenging camera motion, moving supports, and occlusions.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is an intuitive contribution: supervision from an extended object-and-optics mask is transferred to inference with only a tight object mask. The held-out ROSE++ evaluation supports the mechanism, including an optics-region PSNR increase from 19.91 to 27.24 dB over the no-alignment variant while preserving the unedited region.

The empirical package is broad. It includes commercial and open-source comparisons, component ablations, paired object/optics-region evaluation, attention visualization, qualitative examples, and two user studies. Table 2's VACE variants trained on ROSE++ and supplied with the proposed mask provide a particularly informative controlled baseline.

Results on the 200-clip VOIBench are consistently favorable: the method leads five of six headline metrics, with substantial gains in CLIP-I, DINO-I, background consistency, and imaging quality. The qualitative examples also visibly support improved background preservation and occlusion handling.

ROSE++ is a potentially valuable dataset contribution because its source/target/mask/reference quadruplets directly supervise insertion-induced shadows and reflections. Training cost, resolution, iteration count, LoRA rank, inference time, and memory usage are reported, which aids reproducibility.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and candidly identifies the lack of deformable or complex physics-aware interactions as a limitation.
weaknesses: The central geometric claim is less rigorously evaluated than the synthesis component. There is no quantitative mask, trajectory, depth-ordering, or occlusion-boundary evaluation against ground truth, and the scene-flow contribution is supported mainly by one qualitative comparison in Fig. 9. A controlled benchmark against 2D tracking, static-world placement, and alternative 3D propagation methods would make the case substantially stronger.

Several essential implementation details are missing: K in the KNN propagation, how support points are selected instead of nearby occluders, explicit depth testing during reprojection, SAM 2 initialization/refinement, alignment-loss weight and selected transformer layers, and extended-mask thresholds and morphology parameters. These omissions impede reproduction and leave failure behavior ambiguous.

ROSE++ is insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not state its total size, number and provenance of ROSE scenes, train/validation/test split, number of generated candidates, filtering thresholds, or licensing/release details. Reference generation also depends on an ambiguously identified proprietary image-editing model, limiting reproducibility.

The main cross-method comparison is not fully controlled because baselines receive substantially different input modalities: commercial systems receive text prompts, several research systems receive an edited first frame, whereas the proposed method uses a reference image, a 4D mask, and first-frame anchoring. The controlled VACE comparisons mitigate this concern but do not justify all broad superiority claims.

VOIBench is introduced and evaluated by the same authors without ground truth or independent validation. Its object-selection protocol is described only as crawling contextually relevant objects, and no category balance, clip-source licensing, prompt list, or statistical uncertainty is provided. The 25-sample paired ROSE++ test set is also small for the reported optics metrics.

Some interpretations overreach the evidence. Higher multi-view consistency from synthesized references does not by itself demonstrate that the model genuinely infers 4D geometry and lighting, and attention-map expansion is not direct evidence of physically correct shadows or reflections. The method remains a generative plausibility system rather than one that guarantees geometry or optics as stated in the conclusion.

The studies report aggregate preferences but omit confidence intervals, significance tests, participant expertise, and inter-rater agreement. The optics-focused clips were explicitly selected for rich effects, so the selection protocol should be specified to rule out favorable sampling.

Given the paper's applicability to realistic video manipulation and advertising, a brief discussion of deceptive use, provenance, consent, and possible watermarking or disclosure measures would improve the societal-impact treatment.
